passage:
The eel man came down to the dock at Kilcrenan on Thursdays, and on Thursdays Fergal was there before him with the traps already lifted. He was fourteen and had the price in his head before the boat was tied — not the price he wanted, which was one thing, but the price the eel man would pay, which was another, and the whole morning lived in the gap between them.

"Small," the eel man said, tilting the first basket. "Smaller than last week."

"The same," Fergal said. "You had them in a wider basket last week."

The eel man let that pass, which Fergal understood to mean it was true. He turned the eels over with a stick, not hurrying, and Fergal did not hurry him. There was a rule to this that neither of them had ever said aloud: the first man to name a number had already given something away. Fergal watched a gull work the far piling and counted to sixty twice.

"Ninepence the pound," the eel man said at last.

"You sold at one and two in Galway."

"In Galway there is a train." He straightened, and something in his face was almost pleased. "You have been asking."

"I ask," Fergal said.

They settled at elevenpence, which was a penny under what Fergal had decided the night before he would take, and threepence over what the eel man had budgeted on the road up. Neither of them said so. The eel man counted the coins into Fergal's palm slowly, the way a man does when he wants the count to be witnessed, and Fergal did not close his hand until the last one landed.

Afterward the eel man drank his tea on the wall and talked about the weather at Lough Derg, and Fergal answered him properly, because the selling was over and this was a different thing. When the boat pulled out they raised a hand to each other, and each thought, privately and with satisfaction, that he had got the better of the morning.

correct_answer: a bargain in which each side comes away believing it has won
explanation: The closing sentence states that each man thought, privately and with satisfaction, that he had got the better of the morning; the settlement sentence shows why both could think so.

passage:
Every morning before school Marit went down to the tide staff at the end of the town wharf and read the number where the water cut the paint. It was not a difficult job. The staff was marked in tenths of a foot, the black figures ran from nothing at the mud to twelve at the top, and all that was asked of her was to look, to write, and to telephone the reading to the hydrographic office in Rockland before eight o’clock. She had done it for two years.

Her predecessor, a retired weir fisherman named Colby, had told her exactly one thing when he handed over the book: put down what the staff says, not what you expect it to say. In February she had recorded a tide eleven inches below anything in the previous record. The office called back twice to ask whether she was certain, and she said each time that she was, and in the end they entered it.

On the fourth of May a boat she did not know came into the channel and anchored off the ledges, where nobody anchored, because the holding there was poor and everyone local knew it. The boat was white and low and had no name painted on it. A man came out of the wheelhouse with a camera on a strap and photographed the shore in sections, turning a little between each, the way a surveyor works. He did not look at the town. He photographed the fish house, the culvert, the two derelict weirs, and the mouth of the brook. Then he went below, and the boat lay where it was for an hour and left on the ebb.

Marit read the staff at 6:40 — three and four tenths, falling — and telephoned it in. Then, because the book had a column at the right headed REMARKS that she had never once used, she wrote: white boat, no name, anchored off the ledges, photographed the shore, left 7:55.

Nobody ever asked her about it.

a girl whose habit of exact record-keeping leads her to conceal a reading she cannot account for

a girl whose habit of exact record-keeping leads her to correct a mistake made by an earlier observer
a girl whose habit of exact record-keeping leads her to note an event she has no way to interpret
correct_answer: a girl whose habit of exact record-keeping leads her to note an event she has no way to interpret
explanation: Two years of writing down what the staff says, and standing by it in February, are what carry her into using the REMARKS column for a morning she cannot explain and that no one ever asks about.

distractor_rationales.a girl whose habit of exact record-keepi: The staff is never in question; the February reading is confirmed and entered.
She conceals nothing — the entry is written into the official book.
She calls the job easy, not dull, and she performs it that morning as usual.
Colby made no mistake; his one instruction is the rule she follows.

The boat was white and low and had no name painted on it. A man came out of the wheelhouse with a camera on a strap and photographed the shore in sections, turning a little between each, the way a surveyor works. He did not look at the town. He photographed the fish house, the culvert, the two derelict weirs, and the mouth of the brook. Then he went below, and the boat lay where it was for an hour and left on the ebb.

passage:
The plan had been a raft, and Wendy had costed it out on the back of a feed bill: eleven crates from behind the cannery, four lengths of two-by-four that her uncle would not miss, a coil of rope, and two afternoons. The crates were free because the cannery burned them. The two-by-four was free in the sense that nobody had ever counted it. She had drawn the thing twice, once from above and once from the side, and in both drawings it rode high.

It did not ride high. She and Colm got it down the bank on rollers and slid it out, and it went under to the second slat and stopped, sitting in the water like a wet doormat, perfectly steady and perfectly useless, its deck an inch below the river. Colm stepped on and the water came over his shoes.

"It floats," he said, with some justice.

"It floats wrong."

The trouble was the crates. She had assumed fir, which is what the drawing had assumed, and fir is what the cannery used for the light crates that came in holding empty cans. These were the heavy crates, the ones that went out full, made of a dense red wood, close-grained, that had stood in the rain since March and had taken the rain up the way a sponge does. Dry, they might have carried her. Wet, they carried themselves and very little else.

She sat on the bank a while doing the arithmetic she should have done in April, and the arithmetic said eighteen crates, and there were eleven.

So the raft became a float. Tied off the willow and left where it was, an inch under, it was a fine place to land a boat from and a better place to clean fish than the gravel, and by the end of June three families were using it and one of them had put a cleat on it without asking.

passage:
I trim my books with a plough, which is a wooden jaw with a blade in it, cranked across the edge of the text block a few thousandths of an inch at a time. There is a guillotine in a shop twenty minutes’ walk away that would make the same cut in four seconds. People assume I decline it out of sentiment, and I have given up correcting them at parties, but the reason is technical and I would like to set it down once.

A guillotine cuts by descending. It presses the block flat under a clamp, drops a long blade through the whole stack at once, and what it leaves is a face: a single plane, brilliantly square, in which every leaf ends at the same point because every leaf was crushed to the same point first. Release the clamp and the paper breathes back. The face that was square under four hundred pounds of pressure is no longer quite square at rest, and on a thick block of soft paper you can see the recovery — a faint barrelling at the fore edge, most visible where the book is thickest.

A plough cuts by shaving. Each pass takes almost nothing from a block held under a pressure the paper does not resist. Nothing is crushed, so nothing recovers, and the edge you have after the fortieth pass is the edge you will have in thirty years.

I am not claiming the difference is large. On a hardback of machine paper it is invisible, and if you are trimming an edition of two hundred you should use the guillotine and think no more about it. I am claiming that it exists, that it is a property of how each tool works rather than of how carefully you work it, and that once you have seen the barrelling on a book you trimmed yourself you cannot unsee it on anyone else’s. That is a poor argument for a business and a sufficient one for a bench.

correct_answer: defending a preference for one tool by pointing to a difference in what each leaves the paper doing afterward
explanation: The whole argument turns on crushing and recovery: the guillotine’s edge changes when the clamp lifts, the plough’s does not, and the writer says outright that the reason is technical.

The face that was square under four hundred pounds of pressure is no longer quite square at rest, and on a thick block of soft paper you can see the recovery — a faint barrelling at the fore edge, most visible where the book is thickest.

A plough cuts by shaving. Each pass takes almost nothing from a block held under a pressure the paper does not resist. Nothing is crushed, so nothing recovers, and the edge you have after the fortieth pass is the edge you will have in thirty years.

I am not claiming the difference is large. On a hardback of machine paper it is invisible, and if you are trimming an edition of two hundred you should use the guillotine and think no more about it. I am claiming that it exists, that it is a property of how each tool works rather than of how carefully you work it, and that once you have seen the barrelling on a book you trimmed yourself you cannot unsee it on anyone else’s. That is a poor argument for a business and a sufficient one for a bench.

passage:
For two winters I worked the night switchboard at a hotel in Buffalo, eleven to seven, and I came to think of the shift as having four weathers.

Until about one the board is domestic. Guests want ice, or a second pillow, or to know whether the restaurant is really closed, and they ask in the voice people use with a stranger they expect to see at breakfast. I put these through to housekeeping and wrote nothing down.

From one to three the calls come from outside. Someone in another time zone wants room 412 and will not be told that the hotel does not wake guests without a reason; someone’s brother-in-law, drunk and affectionate, wants to sing. This is the only stretch of the night that requires a policy. The policy was mine, since the night manager slept from one thirty and considered the arrangement confidential.

From three to about five the board goes quiet in a way that is not restful. You are alone with the hum of the panel and the knowledge that the next light will not be about ice. In two winters I took four calls in that window that mattered: a chest pain, a woman locked out on a fire escape in February, a man who wanted the name of a hospital and would not say why, and one I still have no category for. The training for these consisted of a laminated card with the fire department’s number, which I never needed, and the switchboard’s own logic, which is that you keep the line open while you find someone.

After five it is staff. The bakery calls to be let in at the loading door, the first taxis want the doorman, a housekeeper phones in sick and you can hear her children behind her.

People ask what the job was like and I say the hours were bad, which is true and is not the answer. The answer is that a building has a pulse, and most people are awake for only one beat of it.
